name: Alabama
climateConsiderations: High summer humidity, heavy Gulf Coast wind/rain loads in mobile/coastal counties, and termite pressure require pressure-treated sill plates and mildew-resistant exterior coatings.
licensingBoardName: Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board
permitNote: Residential projects exceeding $10,000 require a state-licensed residential home builder or Specialty contractor.

name: Alaska
climateConsiderations: Deep frost lines (60–100+ inches), heavy snow loads, permafrost heave, and short summer building windows increase concrete footing and roofing material requirements.
licensingBoardName: Alaska Division of Corporations, Business and Professional Licensing
permitNote: All residential and specialty contractors in Alaska must hold active state registration and bonding.

name: Arizona
climateConsiderations: Intense UV radiation, 110°F+ summer slab curing temperatures, and expansive desert caliche soils require UV-stable elastomeric coatings and early-morning concrete pours.
licensingBoardName: Arizona Registrar of Contractors (AZ ROC)
permitNote: An AZ ROC license is required for any residential project where labor and materials exceed $1,000 or require a building permit.

name: Arkansas
climateConsiderations: Seasonal severe thunderstorms, hail impact risk, and high clay moisture shifts demand impact-rated roof shingles and compacted gravel sub-bases.
licensingBoardName: Arkansas Contractors Licensing Board
permitNote: Home improvement projects over $2,000 are regulated by the Residential Contractors Committee.

name: California
climateConsiderations: Seismic bracing codes, Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) Class A fire-rated roofing/siding rules, Title 24 cool-roof reflectance mandates, and strict South Coast AQMD low-VOC paint limits.
licensingBoardName: California Contractors State License Board (CSLB)
permitNote: California law requires a CSLB license for any construction job totaling $500 or more in combined labor and materials.

name: Colorado
climateConsiderations: Severe Front Range hailstorms (Class 4 UL 2218 impact shingles recommended), high-altitude UV exposure, 36-inch+ frost lines, and bentonite swelling clay soils.
licensingBoardName: Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies (Local Municipal Licensing)
permitNote: General contractors are licensed at the city or county level (e.g., Denver, Colorado Springs, Boulder); roofers must comply with state consumer protection statutes.

name: Connecticut
climateConsiderations: 42-inch frost depth code for deck and fence footings, winter ice-damming requiring 6 feet of eave ice-and-water shield, and coastal wind uplift along Long Island Sound.
licensingBoardName: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection (DCP)
permitNote: All residential remodeling contractors must hold a Connecticut Home Improvement Contractor (HIC) registration.

name: Delaware
climateConsiderations: Coastal salt-air corrosion in Sussex County, high water tables, and mid-Atlantic freeze-thaw cycles require stainless or hot-dipped galvanized exterior fasteners.
licensingBoardName: Delaware Division of Revenue (Contractor Registration)
permitNote: Contractors must register with the Delaware Division of Revenue and obtain county/municipal building permits in New Castle, Kent, or Sussex County.

name: District of Columbia
climateConsiderations: Historic preservation board rules in rowhouse districts, tight urban staging/parking permits, and EPA RRP lead-paint compliance on pre-1978 masonry homes.
licensingBoardName: DC Department of Buildings (DOB)
permitNote: Home improvement contractors must hold a DC Basic Business License in the Home Improvement Contractor category.

name: Florida
climateConsiderations: Florida Building Code (FBC) High-Velocity Hurricane Zone (HVHZ) wind ratings (130–175+ MPH), secondary water barriers, ring-shank roof deck re-nailing, and intense humidity/mildew.
licensingBoardName: Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR)
permitNote: Structural, roofing, and major remodeling require a Florida Certified or Registered Contractor license through the CILB.

name: Georgia
climateConsiderations: Heavy red clay expansion, Formosan and subterranean termite activity, and high summer humidity demand ground-contact UC4A treated lumber and vapor barriers.
licensingBoardName: Georgia State Licensing Board for Residential and General Contractors
permitNote: Residential-Basic or Residential-Light Commercial licenses are required for projects exceeding $2,500 involving structural work.

name: Hawaii
climateConsiderations: Ocean freight surcharges on bulk building materials, severe coastal salt spray corrosion (316 stainless fasteners required), trade-wind uplift, and borate-treated framing lumber codes.
licensingBoardName: Hawaii Contractors License Board (DCCA)
permitNote: A Hawaii contractor license is mandatory for any project where labor and materials exceed $1,500 or require a building permit.

name: Idaho
climateConsiderations: Deep mountain frost lines (36–48 inches), snow load roof engineering, and dry summer cure conditions requiring curing compound on exterior flatwork.
licensingBoardName: Idaho Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses (DOPL)
permitNote: All contractors working on projects valued over $2,000 must register with the Idaho Contractors Board.

name: Illinois
climateConsiderations: 42-inch Chicago-metro frost footing depth, heavy winter road-salt exposure on concrete driveways (air-entrained 4000+ PSI concrete required), and state-mandated roofing licensing.
licensingBoardName: Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR)
permitNote: Roofing contractors must hold a state IDFPR license; general remodeling is licensed at the municipal level.

name: Indiana
climateConsiderations: 40+ annual freeze-thaw cycles require air-entrained exterior concrete, 36-inch frost footings, and ice-and-water shield along roof eaves.
licensingBoardName: Indiana Professional Licensing Agency (County/City Contractor Licensing)
permitNote: Contractor licensing is administered by local county and city building departments (e.g., Indianapolis/Marion County).

name: Iowa
climateConsiderations: 42–48 inch frost line code, straight-line wind/derecho shingle uplift resistance, and expansive glacial till subgrades.
licensingBoardName: Iowa Division of Labor — Contractor Registration
permitNote: Every construction contractor earning at least $2,000 annually in Iowa must register with the state.

name: Kansas
climateConsiderations: High wind and hail frequency across the Great Plains (impact-resistant Class 4 shingles earn insurance discounts) and seasonal shrink-swell clay soils.
licensingBoardName: Kansas Attorney General — Roofing Registration & Local Building Codes
permitNote: Roofing contractors must register with the Kansas Attorney General; general contractors are licensed by city/county.

name: Kentucky
climateConsiderations: Karst limestone terrain drainage, humid summers, and winter freeze-thaw transitions require proper gutter drainage away from foundations.
licensingBoardName: Kentucky Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction
permitNote: Local municipalities (such as Louisville Metro and Lexington) issue residential contractor licenses and permits.

name: Louisiana
climateConsiderations: Hurricane wind uplift codes (FORTIFIED Roof standards incentivize insurance savings), expansive alluvial clay soils, and Formosan termite protection.
licensingBoardName: Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors (LSLBC)
permitNote: Home improvement projects exceeding $7,500 require LSLBC registration; projects over $50,000 require a residential license.

name: Maine
climateConsiderations: 48–60 inch frost depth for deck piers, 50–90 psf ground snow load roof framing, coastal salt exposure, and deep winter ice-dam protection.
licensingBoardName: Maine Office of Professional and Occupational Regulation
permitNote: Maine requires written home construction contracts for any residential job exceeding $3,000 under the Home Construction Contracts Act.

name: Maryland
climateConsiderations: Chesapeake Bay critical-area impervious surface limits (permeable pavers often favored), humid summers, and 30-inch frost footings.
licensingBoardName: Maryland Home Improvement Commission (MHIC)
permitNote: Anyone performing residential remodeling in Maryland must hold an active MHIC license.

name: Massachusetts
climateConsiderations: Strict Massachusetts 780 CMR building code, 48-inch frost footings, coastal Nor’easter wind loads, and mandatory lead-safe renovation rules on older housing stock.
licensingBoardName: Massachusetts Office of Consumer Affairs and Business Regulation (OCABR)
permitNote: Most residential work requires both a Construction Supervisor License (CSL) and a Home Improvement Contractor (HIC) registration.

name: Michigan
climateConsiderations: 42-inch minimum frost depth statewide, heavy lake-effect snow loads, and severe freeze-thaw cycles requiring 6-inch compacted gravel bases under patios and driveways.
licensingBoardName: Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA)
permitNote: A Michigan Residential Builder or Maintenance & Alteration (M&A) license is required for projects of $600 or more.

name: Minnesota
climateConsiderations: 42–60 inch frost footing requirements, strict attic vapor barrier and ice-dam ventilation rules, and sub-zero winter thermal expansion gaps on exterior siding and decking.
licensingBoardName: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry (DLI)
permitNote: Residential building contractors and remodelers must be licensed by Minnesota DLI if they perform two or more trade skills.

name: Mississippi
climateConsiderations: Expansive Yazoo clay soils in central Mississippi, Gulf Coast hurricane wind codes, and high year-round moisture requiring mildew-algicide roof shingles.
licensingBoardName: Mississippi State Board of Contractors (MSBOC)
permitNote: A Mississippi Residential Remodeling license is required when project costs exceed $10,000.

name: Missouri
climateConsiderations: Wide seasonal temperature swings (-10°F to 100°F+), severe spring hail, and plastic clay subsoils requiring reinforced concrete slabs and 30–36 inch footings.
licensingBoardName: Missouri Division of Professional Registration (Local Municipal Licensing)
permitNote: Contractor licensing and permits are issued by local jurisdictions such as St. Louis County, Kansas City, and Springfield.

name: Montana
climateConsiderations: 48-inch frost lines, high Chinook wind gusts along the Rocky Mountain Front, and heavy mountain snow loads.
licensingBoardName: Montana Department of Labor & Industry — Construction Contractor Registration
permitNote: All construction contractors with employees or independent contractor exemptions must register with Montana DLI.

name: Nebraska
climateConsiderations: High plains hail frequency, 42-inch frost depth, and wind-driven rain requiring starter strip adhesive and Class 4 impact shingles.
licensingBoardName: Nebraska Department of Labor — Contractor Registration
permitNote: All contractors doing business in Nebraska must register with the Nebraska Department of Labor.

name: Nevada
climateConsiderations: Extreme desert heat and low humidity in Clark County cause rapid concrete surface evaporation (plastic shrinkage cracking) unless evaporation retarders and wet curing are used.
licensingBoardName: Nevada State Contractors Board (NSCB)
permitNote: A Nevada contractor license is required for any job over $1,000 or any project requiring a building permit.

name: New Hampshire
climateConsiderations: 48-inch deep frost footings, granite ledge excavation challenges, and 60+ psf snow load requirements on roofs and decks.
licensingBoardName: New Hampshire Office of Professional Licensure and Certification
permitNote: General contractors are regulated via local town building permits following the New Hampshire State Building Code.

name: New Jersey
climateConsiderations: Coastal windborne debris zones along the Jersey Shore, 36-inch frost lines, and strict municipal zoning/impervious coverage caps on patios and driveways.
licensingBoardName: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs
permitNote: Every residential contractor must register as a New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (HIC) and display their registration number.

name: New Mexico
climateConsiderations: High-altitude UV degradation on stains and paints, stucco/adobe elastomeric crack bridging, and monsoon flash drainage.
licensingBoardName: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department — Construction Industries Division (CID)
permitNote: New Mexico CID requires GB-2 residential or specialty contractor licensing for nearly all construction work.

name: New York
climateConsiderations: Upstate lake-effect snow loads (up to 70+ psf) and 48-inch frost depths vs NYC/Long Island high labor rates, co-op insurance requirements, and coastal wind codes.
licensingBoardName: New York Department of State / Local County Consumer Affairs
permitNote: Home improvement licenses are strictly enforced at the county/city level (NYC DCWP, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester, Putnam, Rockland, Erie).

name: North Carolina
climateConsiderations: Piedmont red clay grading, coastal 130+ MPH wind zones on the Outer Banks/Wilmington, and high summer humidity requiring breathable exterior finishes.
licensingBoardName: North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors (NCLBGC)
permitNote: A North Carolina General Contractor license is required for any project costing $40,000 or more.

name: North Dakota
climateConsiderations: Extreme winter lows (-30°F), 48–72 inch frost footing depths, expansive Red River Valley clay, and short exterior concrete/painting seasons.
licensingBoardName: North Dakota Secretary of State — Contractor Licensing
permitNote: A North Dakota Contractor License (Class A, B, C, or D) is required for any job exceeding $4,000.

name: Ohio
climateConsiderations: 32–42 inch frost line depth from south to north, Lake Erie wind and snow loads, and de-icing salt scaling protection on concrete flatwork.
licensingBoardName: Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board (OCILB) & Local Municipalities
permitNote: General remodeling contractors register with local city/county building departments (Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati).

name: Oklahoma
climateConsiderations: Severe spring hail and tornado corridor wind uplift (high-wind 6-nail shingle fastening and Class 4 impact shingles strongly recommended) and expansive red clay.
licensingBoardName: Oklahoma Construction Industries Board (CIB)
permitNote: Roofing contractors must be registered and endorsed by the Oklahoma CIB; general contractors follow municipal permit rules.

name: Oregon
climateZone: IECC Zones 4C–5B (Marine West Coast to Cool-Dry)
climateConsiderations: Persistent Willamette Valley and coastal rain requires rainscreen siding drainage gaps, moss-resistant zinc/copper roof strips, and moisture-tolerant deck stains.
licensingBoardName: Oregon Construction Contractors Board (CCB)
permitNote: Anyone working for compensation on any home improvement activity in Oregon must hold an active CCB license and bond.

name: Pennsylvania
climateConsiderations: 36–48 inch frost footing depths, historic stone/brick masonry pointing considerations, and winter freeze-thaw cycles.
licensingBoardName: Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General — Home Improvement Contractor Registration (HICPA)
permitNote: Contractors performing more than $5,000 of residential work per year must register under HICPA with the PA Attorney General.

name: Rhode Island
climateConsiderations: 120–140 MPH coastal wind design speeds in Narragansett Bay communities, salt-air fastener corrosion, and 40-inch frost lines.
licensingBoardName: Rhode Island Contractors’ Registration and Licensing Board (CRLB)
permitNote: All residential contractors and remodelers must register with the Rhode Island CRLB and carry required liability insurance.

name: South Carolina
climateConsiderations: Coastal hurricane wind and seismic zones around Charleston, high summer humidity, and sandy coastal vs Upstate red clay soil prep.
licensingBoardName: South Carolina Residential Builders Commission (LLR)
permitNote: A South Carolina Residential Builder license or specialty registration is required for jobs exceeding $200.

name: South Dakota
climateConsiderations: 48-inch frost lines, frequent hailstorms across the plains and Black Hills, and high wind uplift.
licensingBoardName: South Dakota Municipal Building Departments (Sioux Falls, Rapid City)
permitNote: Residential contractor licenses are issued at the municipal level and require state excise tax registration.

name: Tennessee
climateConsiderations: Shallow limestone bedrock in Middle/East Tennessee, New Madrid seismic zone in West Tennessee, and humid summer algae growth on roofs and decks.
licensingBoardName: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
permitNote: Projects $25,000 or more require a state Contractor License; projects $3,000–$24,999 in covered counties require a Home Improvement license.

name: Texas
climateConsiderations: Highly expansive Blackland Prairie clay soils (rebar-reinforced concrete slabs essential), Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA) Gulf Coast roof certifications, and severe North Texas hail.
licensingBoardName: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR) / Local Municipal Permits
permitNote: General and roofing contractors register at the city level (Houston, Dallas, Austin, San Antonio); Gulf Coast roofs require a TDI WPI-8 windstorm certificate.

name: Utah
climateConsiderations: Wasatch Front seismic fault zones, heavy mountain bench snow loads, 30–42 inch frost depths, and intense high-elevation UV exposure.
licensingBoardName: Utah Division of Professional Licensing (DOPL)
permitNote: A Utah DOPL B100, R100, or specialty S-series contractor license is required for projects exceeding $3,000.

name: Vermont
climateConsiderations: 54–60 inch frost depth for deck and fence footings, heavy wet snow loads, and strict Act 250 / local energy stretch codes.
licensingBoardName: Vermont Office of Professional Regulation — Residential Contractors
permitNote: Residential contractors must register with the Vermont Secretary of State for projects valued at $10,000 or more.

name: Virginia
climateConsiderations: Tidewater coastal wind zones, Piedmont shrink-swell clay, and Northern Virginia HOA architectural review and county permit standards.
licensingBoardName: Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation (DPOR)
permitNote: Virginia requires a Class C license for jobs over $1,000, Class B for $10,000+, and Class A for $120,000+.

name: Washington
climateZone: IECC Zones 4C–5B (Marine West Coast to Cool-Dry)
climateConsiderations: Continuous Puget Sound moisture requiring rainscreen siding furring strips, seismic hold-downs, moss prevention on roofs, and Washington State Energy Code (WSEC) insulation levels.
licensingBoardName: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries (L&I)
permitNote: All general and specialty contractors in Washington must register with L&I, carry a surety bond, and maintain general liability insurance.

name: West Virginia
climateConsiderations: Steep hillside grading and retaining wall drainage requirements, mountain snow loads, and 30–36 inch frost lines.
licensingBoardName: West Virginia Division of Labor — Contractor Licensing Board
permitNote: A West Virginia Contractor License is required for residential projects valued at $5,000 or more.

name: Wisconsin
climateConsiderations: 48-inch frost depth code for footings, deep eave ice-dam protection (2 rows of ice-and-water shield), and air-entrained concrete for driveway salt resistance.
licensingBoardName: Wisconsin Department of Safety and Professional Services (DSPS)
permitNote: One- and two-family dwelling contractors must hold a Wisconsin Dwelling Contractor and Dwelling Contractor Qualifier credential.

name: Wyoming
climateConsiderations: Sustained 60–90+ MPH winter wind gusts requiring 6-nail high-wind shingle installation, 42–48 inch frost depths, and rapid dry-air concrete evaporation.
licensingBoardName: Wyoming Municipal Building Departments (Cheyenne, Casper, Laramie)
permitNote: Contractor licensing and building permits are managed by local city and county building departments.
